answers: An operation in London has given 9-year-old Kieran Sorkin a pair of ears—made from his ribs, no less. Born deaf with no ears, Kieran was able to hear because of an implanted hearing aid, but he still wanted ears. "I want people to stop asking me questions," he told the BBC. "I'd like just to look like my friends. I'd also like to be able to wear sunglasses and earphones." So surgeons traced an outline of Kieran's mom's ears, removed cartilage from the boy's ribs, and sliced, contoured, and sewed the cartilage. Then they put it in two skin pockets and vacuumed them into the shape of ears. They don't perform any function, but Kieran's plastic surgeon says they can deliver a huge confidence boost: "If you can change the confidence of a patient at this young age, you can change their whole trajectory in life," he said. The ears should last, too, because they're made of cartilage rather than prosthetics, the Guardian reports. Every year about 100 British newborns lack one or both ears (it's called microtia), and the hospital Kieran went to performs the operation about 40 times a year. Scientists hope to one day make ears from the fat tissue of patients, instead of ribs. Kieran might have liked that, since he got so excited on seeing his new ears that he cried "Wow!" and giggled—which made his ribs hurt from the operation. full.prediction:
**Summary of News Passages:**

A nine-year-old boy named Kieran Sorkin, born with a rare condition called bilateral microtia, has undergone a groundbreaking reconstructive surgery at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London. Kieran was born without fully formed ears, only having small earlobes, and also suffered from hearing loss. However, thanks to previous surgeries and the use of a hearing aid, he has been able to hear, though he remains about 90% deaf. His parents, David and Louise Sorkin, have long supported his desire to have ears that look like those of his peers, a wish he expressed since the age of six after watching a TV program about the procedure.

The surgery, which took six hours, involved harvesting cartilage from Kieran’s ribs and shaping it into new ear frameworks. The surgeons used an outline of his mother’s ears as a "family template" to ensure the new ears closely resembled his natural ear shape. The ears were then grafted onto Kieran’s head and shaped using suction. The procedure was primarily cosmetic, though it has had a significant psychological impact on Kieran, boosting his confidence and improving his social interactions. Kieran had previously struggled at school due to his appearance, but he has now moved to a school with a deafness unit in every year group, where he feels more accepted.

The surgery was performed by consultant plastic and reconstructive surgeon Neil Bulstrode, who emphasized the importance of creating balanced ears to enhance the patient’s quality of life. He noted that such procedures can have a profound effect on a child’s confidence and future trajectory. Kieran will require a follow-up operation in six months to further refine the shape of his ears, but the results so far have been highly successful.

Looking to the future, researchers at the University College London Institute for Child Health are exploring the use of stem cells to grow new ear frameworks from a child’s own fat tissue. This method would be less invasive than the current rib cartilage harvesting technique. While this technology is still in its early stages, it holds promise for more advanced and less painful reconstructive procedures in the coming years.

Kieran’s parents expressed their joy and relief at the successful outcome, noting that the surgery has not only improved his appearance but also his self-esteem. Kieran himself was thrilled with the results, exclaiming “Wow!” upon seeing his new ears. The procedure has marked a significant milestone in the treatment of microtia, offering hope for other children with similar conditions.
